doc.title: Kenny Davern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Why clarinet: Artie Shaw, an Albert System horn and teacher Mr. Bruno
summary: He wanted piano or trumpet, heard Artie Shaw's concerto, and got a $35 C clarinet in Albert System taught by Louis Bruno, switching to Boehm at 13.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the first horn: clarinet and saxophone beginnings

blocks.x: What put a clarinet in your hands as a young kid?

The fact, one I couldn’t figure out how to play a trumpet, and we couldn’t afford a piano. That was my first love was the piano. Second I wanted to learn the trumpet. I didn’t know how you could get all those notes out of just three valves, there was something wrong with that picture. I mean math was not my strong point. Then I heard Artie Shaw play the Clarinet Concerto on the radio. I guess this had to be about 1945 or 6. And I fantasized. This instrument was sailing over the whole band and I liked that whole concept. Plus it was made of wood, which was part of a growing tree at one time, all kinds of romantic ideas that came in my head. And well lo and behold we got a clarinet. But it was a $35 one at the time and it was a C clarinet and an Albert System.

Yeah. And an Albert System. And we couldn’t find anybody to teach me, because it was an old fashioned system and practically everybody played the Boehm, and we did find an old Italian teacher, which was on the line where Brooklyn and Queens meet you see, his name was Mr. Bruno. Louis Bruno. Or Luigi Bruno. And he taught both systems, Albert and Boehm system clarinet.
Well you eventually had to make a transition, right?
Yeah I did. At 13 I made the transition. But I guess I must have spent maybe three years playing an Albert System clarinet, which I later went back to and I switched again.
